q: The photon energy of green light is about $2.5\,\text{eV}$ and the maximum photon energy of dental X-rays about $60\,\text{keV}$. Which can ionise a water molecule, whose ionisation energy is $12.6\,\text{eV}$, and why does brighter green light not change this?
a: Only the X-ray photon, because its energy exceeds the ionisation energy many times over. The energy of a single green photon, $2.5\,\text{eV}$, is too small, and brighter light only means more photons of the same kind: a single photon still cannot remove an electron.

q: Medical supplies are sterilised with gamma radiation. Do they become radioactive?
a: No. Gamma radiation ionises atoms and kills microbes by breaking their molecules. In ordinary sterilisation, for example with the gamma radiation of cobalt-60, the photon energy is not enough to change nuclei, so the supplies do not become radioactive. Radioactivity can arise mainly from neutron radiation. Gamma radiation can still be dangerous without radioactive contamination: near a strong gamma source the whole body is exposed to penetrating external radiation, even if no radioactive material gets onto the skin or into the body. That is why the source of a sterilisation plant is behind thick shielding.
